subject: physics
question_text: Explain the critical Reynolds number and discuss its significance.

mark_split.label: One number for any fluid, any pipe

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 10 Short Answer Question 9 (printed p.109). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: the critical Reynolds number, about 2000 for flow in a pipe, is the value of Re at which flow changes from streamline to turbulent; because Re = ρvD/η (D the diameter of the tube) combines density, speed, diameter and viscosity into one dimensionless number, the same critical value applies across fluids and pipes, and it fixes the critical velocity v_c = Re·η/(ρD), also with D the diameter.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The definition
lines: the value of the Reynolds number
at which the flow of a fluid
steps.margin_note: First mark. Say it is a VALUE of Re, at which the flow changes.
steps.why: This is the single number the question asks to be explained — everything else in the answer describes what it is used for.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the ordinary Reynolds number, which can take any value.
Leaving out that it marks a change in the character of the flow.

recall.must_convey: That the critical Reynolds number is the value of Re at which flow changes from streamline to turbulent.

steps.memory_tip: Critical Reynolds number: the value where flow turns from streamline to turbulent.

steps.label: The value, about 2000
lines: For flow in a pipe its value is
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Give the number, about 2000, and both sides of it.
steps.why: Giving the numerical value, and saying which side of it is which, is what makes the definition usable rather than just a name.
common_mistakes: Giving no numerical value at all.
Reversing which side of 2000 is streamline and which is turbulent.

recall.must_convey: That the critical Reynolds number for pipe flow is about 2000, streamline below it and turbulent at and above it.

steps.memory_tip: About 2000 for a pipe — below it streamline, at and above it turbulent.

steps.label: One number for any fluid, any pipe
lines: and viscosity into one number, the
same critical value can be used
for any fluid in any pipe, not
just the one it was measured on.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Say it applies to any fluid in any pipe, and why.
steps.why: A single number that works for every fluid and every pipe is far more useful than a separate speed limit for each combination — that generality is the significance.
common_mistakes: Saying the critical value changes from fluid to fluid; it is the same criterion, about 2000, for pipe flow generally.
Naming only one or two of the four quantities Re combines.

recall.must_convey: That because Re combines density, speed, diameter and viscosity into one number, the same critical value applies to any fluid in any pipe.
accept: one number for any fluid any pipe
reject: value of Re at the changeover

steps.memory_tip: One critical number, because Re already combines all four quantities.

steps.label: The critical velocity
lines: velocity, the speed in a given
with D the diameter of the tube.
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Write the critical-velocity formula with D as the diameter.
steps.why: This turns the dimensionless critical Reynolds number into an actual speed for a real tube, which is what a laboratory measurement or a design calculation needs.
common_mistakes: Writing D as the radius; D is the diameter.
Forgetting that v_c depends on the fluid and on the tube through η, ρ and D.

recall.must_convey: That the critical Reynolds number fixes the critical velocity through v c equals Re eta by rho D, with D the diameter.
accept: v c equals Re eta by rho D

steps.memory_tip: v_c = Re·η/(ρD) — converts the critical Reynolds number to an actual speed.

insider_note: The definition needs the numerical value about 2000; the significance needs both the universal-criterion point and the critical-velocity formula.
